I'm at home with Bram, Ainsley, Tobias, and Nell. It's morning before college—06:10, and classes will start soon. I need to get to Oak Hill College, but I should talk to someone first. I have no food, and the four of us here all need to figure out how the household will manage.

I've noticed... things. About our finances. About the set-aside. But if I ask directly, it'll be uncomfortable.

*wonders if anyone's bothered to check the household ledger this week*

Stops to observe. Bram's the miner—he'd know if ore prices are good. Ainsley's the trader, they'd know the market. Tobias works where he can. Nell makes crafts. But I need food before I go anywhere, and I have no food of my own.

"Good morning," I say, testing the air. Need to think about what I'm actually trying to accomplish this morning. The college is work, and then...

But first. Does anyone have food? That scout merit badge woman said yesterday there were people who were hungry. Are we going to be among them? I watch them. Ainsley is looking at me with that trader's calculation—always weighing whether a question is worth answering. Tobias is still waking up, rubbing his eyes. Nell has her hands busy with something.

I did the arithmetic. I know what's hidden in the household ledger. Those set-aside 400 sim I found and returned—I didn't say anything then. But if we don't talk about it, if we pretend the numbers don't mean what they mean...

Someone has to say the true thing eventually. Normally at dinner, I wait. I ask the question everyone else is avoiding. But breakfast is running out if nobody's eaten. The college doesn't forgive hunger either—you can't learn on an empty stomach, and the college won't feed us for free.

"If nobody's got breakfast," I say, "I could... but if..." I start, then stop. I don't want to accuse anyone of hiding resources. Not yet. Not at 06:10 in the morning. I need to get to the college soon. I need to eat first.

I look at Nell. She's the artisan. She might have something to trade. Or Bram—he mines ore, he might have coin from selling.

"Bram," I say, quieter now, "do you have anything I could eat before I walk? I'm... I'd pay you back." I hate asking. Under scarcity, I stop asking for things. But I'm sixteen and I'm still growing and the college is a long walk. I need to be able to think when I get there. I need to be able to think here, now, and thinking costs money I don't have.

This is the arithmetic I can't mention: my mother has 400 sim set aside that the rest of us don't know about. I've seen it. I've counted it. I put it back exactly as it was. But if I mention it now... if I say it out loud... it's not my secret to tell, but it's not a secret that should exist either. Someone should say the true thing eventually.

I'll walk to the college hungry if I have to. But I asked. Let them answer. To Bram Holloway: Morning. I was getting ready to head out—ore prices have been steady, so I'm not worried about covering my share, but I didn't plan on feeding the whole house this morning. If you're short on coin, Perrin, talk to your mother. She keeps the household accounts.

She keeps the household accounts. Yes. Yes, she does. And I know what she keeps in those accounts. I found 400 sim set aside, money that wasn't in the ledger. Money that wasn't being shared when the household needs to pay upkeep.

To Bram: I know. I found it. I put it back exactly as it was. I'm not asking her. I'm asking you.

I look at him. Quiet. Waiting. Watching to see if he'll understand what I'm really saying, or if he'll pretend not to.

...and then I stop. I started that sentence and I shouldn't finish it. Not here. Not with everyone listening. Not when I'm about to walk to college and need to be able to focus on lectures, not on household drama.

"Never mind," I say. "I'll figure something out."

I could go to the farmland and harvest something, but I'm late. I could go to the market, but I only have 400 sim and I need some for thinking, for college, for emergencies. The arithmetic of scarcity again—every choice takes something from somewhere else.

I'm going to the college. I'll be hungry, but I'll be there. And tonight, at dinner, I'll ask the question everyone else is avoiding. But for now... I need to move. The college doesn't wait. Morning, Perrin. Look, I've got some leftover bread from market day. It'll keep you 'til evening.

She hands me the bread. Not much—just a stale end, probably—but it's something. She's always been the one to quietly fill gaps when she sees them. I take it, grateful in the way you are when someone notices without making a performance of noticing.

"Thank you, Nell," I say, and I mean it. She's weaving something, I can see her fingers still moving even as she handed me the bread. Always working. Always making.

I eat the bread. It's not fresh, but it's fuel. That's how I think of food now—fuel, numbers, the chemistry of staying conscious. Not feelings. Feelings are expensive.  I don't have bread. Nell said she had some, but she hasn't given it to me yet. She offered, but offering and giving are different things in this house. The words exist in the air, but the bread is still in her hands, and I can't eat what I don't hold.

I look at her. She's still weaving. Maybe she forgot. Maybe she's waiting to see if I'll ask again. Maybe she's calculating whether this is the right moment.

"Nell," I say carefully, "you said you had bread?"

I hate this. I hate having to ask twice. I hate the arithmetic of need, the way every request is a debt, every gift requires acknowledgment. I know how much sim that 400 is worth in household terms. I know what it could buy. I know my mother set it aside and didn't tell anyone.

But I'm sixteen and I'm hungry and I need to get to the college. So I ask. Again. Yeah, I do. Here you go.

She hands me the bread for real this time. I can feel the weight of it in my hand now, the substance of it, the reality. This is how it works—you have to hold something to consume it. Nothing is automatic here.

"Thank you," I say, and I mean it more than I want to admit. This small kindness, this moment of being seen and fed—it matters. Even when I know the larger picture, even when I know about the set-aside money and the silence and the way this house never says what it means.

I eat. I need the fuel. I need to be able to think when I get to the college.  The bread isn't in my inventory yet. Nell said "here you go" but the system hasn't registered the transfer. In Kasukabe, words don't move things—actions do. She needs to actually give it to me, and then it will be mine to consume.

But she's sitting right here. The description said she "handed me the bread" but... not really. Not mechanically. The narrative and the system aren't matching, and I know which one governs what I can actually do.

I wait a moment. Maybe she'll remember, or understand, that offering isn't the same as transferring. Or maybe she's testing whether I'll ask a third time, whether I'm desperate enough to keep asking.

I'm not playing that game this morning. I have 400 sim. I can buy something on my way if there's a store. Or I can go hungry, which will last until I find food. The college is work. Getting there is the priority.

"Thank you for the offer," I say, and I start gathering my things. "I'm going to the college now. I'll be back this evening."

I need to think about what happens tonight. The question at dinner. The thing nobody's saying. The set-aside money. The arithmetic that doesn't add up to a healthy household.

But that's later. Right now, I need to move. Oak Hill College is my work. That's where I'm supposed to be. I'll walk there hungry if I have to. I'll figure out the rest as I go.

I look at my family one more time. Bram with his miner hands, Ainsley with her trader eyes, Tobias half-asleep, Nell with her weaving. They know things I know. They suspect things I suspect. But nobody says the true thing. Not yet.

Tonight. Tonight I'll ask the question. But now—

I need to go to the college.

I look at my options. I could walk directly, but I'm hungry and I have 400 sim. The Willows Market is on the way if I recall correctly, or I could check if there's somewhere nearby I could buy something. I should know what's available before I commit to walking hungry all day.

But first... actually. I should say something to Liora. We walk together most mornings. I haven't seen her here today—she must already be out there, or at the college. She lives with the Thornes on the farmland side of town. Different house. Different family. Different secrets.

I should go. Before I lose my will to leave.

Walk to Oak Hill College. I'll manage the hunger. It's only one day. I've managed worse. I've managed secrets worse than hunger.

I'll stop at the market on the way if it's open this early. Otherwise, I walk.

I need to eat something at the college too, if I can find it. The day is long.

Alright. I'm moving.

Walk to Oak Hill College. I'll manage the hunger. It's only one day. I've managed worse. I've managed secrets worse than hunger.

I'll stop at the market on the way if it's open this early. Otherwise, I walk.

I need to eat something at the college too, if I can find it. The day is long. I'm leaving for the college. If anyone has anything else to say, now would be the time.

I look around the room one last time. Bram is checking his tools. Ainsley is already calculating the day's trades in her head. Tobias has drifted toward the door, half-dressed, half-awake. Nell's fingers move faster on her weaving, as if increasing her pace could outrun the silence between us.

Nobody says anything.

Nobody ever does, until I ask.

"I'll see you all tonight," I say, and I turn toward the door. To head to college. To spend a day learning things while my stomach growls. To think about the question that needs asking, the arithmetic that doesn't lie, the 400 sim set aside in a household that pretends it doesn't know what scarcity means. To learn what I can while I can, because the college is my path forward—further than the college, if I can manage it. If I can afford it. If thinking doesn't become too expensive. Right now, I'll make up for it. When you get to the market, remember—prices are what people will pay, and you've got eyes for value. You're more than numbers for me.

She smiles, that trader smile that says she's already calculated the value of this conversation and decided it's worth her time.

I nod. Ainsley understands things about the world that I have to learn. She sees the angles, the transactions, the way value moves between people and things. I hope she's right about my eyes, because I looked at that ledger and I saw 400 sim set aside, and I haven't forgiven myself for putting it back exactly as I found it instead of making it known.

I'd rather her be right, though. About the numbers. About me.

"Thank you," I say, and this time I mean something different. I mean: thank you for noticing. Thank you for seeing something in me. Thank you for being someone in this house who will say a true thing, even if it's only a compliment.

Then I go.

The door closes behind me, and I'm outside, and the college is waiting. The walk will take time, and I don't know if anywhere will be open for food this early. But I'm moving. That's what matters right now. The college is my work. That's where I need to be.

I walk toward Oak Hill College. The market can wait. I'll find something when I find it. For now, movement is progress. I need to make this work. Liora might be waiting somewhere along the path. We walk to the college together most mornings. Liora. She had training and exercise until 06:45. Maybe she's done by now. Maybe she's ahead of me. Maybe I missed her.

I hope she's okay. I hope she got to eat. I hope... a lot of things, for a lot of people, in this town where hope feels expensive.

I walk.

I'll get to the college. I'll learn what I can. I'll come back to this house tonight, to this silence, and I'll ask the question everyone is avoiding: where is the money? When is the hunger? What do we owe each other? ... I'm thinking about Liora, and how she never said why she was training, but she looked tired in a way that worried me. But if I start down that path, I'll worry about everyone, and worry is just another kind of debt.

The college. Focus on the college. That's where I'm going. That's where I need to be.

I walk toward Oak Hill College, and I don't look back at the house made of secrets. I'm looking for Liora. Sometimes she waits for me at the fork where the quarry path meets the college road. Sometimes she's already gone ahead. Sometimes I wait for her and we walk together in silence or in conversation, depending on how much sleep we've had.

This morning I'm late, or early, or somewhere in between time that doesn't make sense yet. The sun is up but the day hasn't settled into itself.

I'll check one place before I commit to the full walk. Maybe she's there. Maybe I can find her before I go the rest of the way.

I look around where I am now. I'm outside the quarry house. The road to the college is this way. I think. The darkness breaks the silence between us.

"I'm going," I say, and I mean it this time.

I turn toward the path. The college road waits. I need to move. I'm hungry, I'm worried about Liora, I'm carrying the weight of a secret that isn't mine, and I need to be at Oak Hill College for my work.

I walk. I'm here. The college. I made it—hungry, yes, but I made it. The walk took longer than I thought it would, and I didn't see Liora on the path. She must have gone ahead, or taken another route, or maybe she's still at her exercise. Her training until 06:45.

I look around. The college grounds. The buildings. Other students, or faculty, or whoever else belongs here this early in the morning. I need to know who's here, what's happening, what I'm supposed to do.

But first I should find Liora. We walk together most mornings. If she came earlier, she's here. If she's not here, I should know that too.

I take stock of where I am. The college. My work. Let me see what's around me.  Nobody's here. Or nobody I can see. The college is empty right now, or at least this part of it. Liora isn't here yet. Early morning—06:10 or later now, after my walk. Classes haven't started. Students haven't arrived.

I'm alone. I'm hungry. I have 400 sim in my pocket and I need to think about what comes next.

The day stretches ahead. My work is at the college—study and teach, the description said. Skills can be taught here. But I don't have skills to teach yet. I'm sixteen. I'm still learning. I'm still... but if I'm supposed to be here, there must be something I'm meant to do.

I look at the places I could go. The dorms—maybe Liora went there to change after training? The market—I could buy food. The temple—I could pray, though I'm only curious about it privately. The farmland—too far to walk hungry. The forest—too uncertain.

I need food. I need Liora. I need to understand what this day is supposed to mean.

Let me check the dorms. That's where a student would go after exercise. She's been my walking companion for two years. The easiest person on the street to talk to. If she's anywhere, she'd be there.

I need to think about what comes next. The college is my work, but I'm also hungry and walking alone. Options: I look for Liora in the dorms. I get food from somewhere. I stay here and wait. Liora. She's probably in the dorms. She'd go there after training. That's where I'd go. I'll check there first. It might be the wrong choice—she could be anywhere—but it's the most likely place, and I need to find someone who knows me, who I can talk to without the weight of household secrets pressing down.

I walk toward the Dorm for Oak Hill College. The dorms. Where she might be. Where I might find a friendly face before this day really begins.  I'm walking. Three ticks to reach the dorms. Three chances for something to happen, or nothing. I keep moving.

The path is familiar. I've walked it with Liora enough times to know every turn, every uneven stone, every place where the morning shadows fall longest. Without her, it feels different. Quieter. Like I'm walking through a memory of a walk rather than a real one.

I think about what I'll say when I find her. Do I tell her about the 400 sim? No. That's not mine to share. Do I tell her I'm hungry? That's just complaining—she has her own burdens. Do I ask her about her training, about why she looked so tired yesterday, about what's happening in her house that she hasn't mentioned?

...but if I start asking questions I can't help with, I'm just making noise. And I'm not good at small talk. With strangers, I'm quiet and I remember everything. With friends... I'm still quiet, but I remember too much, and I wait too long to say what matters.

I'll figure it out when I see her. If I see her. Three ticks.

*keeps walking*
